discussions.name: NWS Seattle
synopsis: Split flow aloft over Western Washington today. Flow aloft consolidating tonight with a weather system approaching the coast. The system will move by to the south and weaken Wednesday and Wednesday night. High amplitude upper level ridge building offshore Thursday with dry northerly flow aloft developing by Thursday night. Ridge moves over the area Friday before getting pinched off Friday night. Next system stalling off the coast over the weekend.
hydrology: No river flooding expected in the next 7 days.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: Split flow aloft over Western Washington today. Flow aloft consolidating tonight with a weather system approaching the coast. The system will move by to the south and weaken Wednesday and Wednesday night. High amplitude upper level ridge building offshore Thursday with dry northerly flow aloft developing by Thursday night. Ridge moves over the area Friday before getting pinched off Friday night. Next system stalling off the coast over the weekend.

sections.title: Short term (today through Thursday)
paragraphs: No forecast updates are anticipated this morning with some partial sunshine expected by afternoon. The next system offshore is still expected to track mainly south of the area with some light wrap around precip making into the southern half of the CWA tomorrow afternoon and evening. Previous discussion follows with update to aviation portion.

Satellite imagery shows mostly cloudy skies over Western Washington early this morning. Doppler radar has some last gasp showers along the coast. Fog has formed over the Southwest Interior and along the Kitsap peninsula with visibilities below a mile in some locations. Temperatures at 3 AM/11Z were in the mid 30s to lower 40s.

Split flow aloft over Western Washington today as the next weather system approaches the area well offshore. Residual moisture left behind from the upper level trough that moved through Monday evening will be tough to get rid of this morning without any ridge building over the area. The layer is shallow so by afternoon expect less cloud cover and fog and more sunshine. Highs near 50.

Mostly clear skies tonight with the next system moving southeast offshore. Clear skies and light flow over the interior lowlands leading to more fog especially south of Seattle. Freezing fog possible over the Southwest Interior with low temperatures near freezing. Lows elsewhere in the mid 30s to lower 40s. Low level offshore flow increasing in the foothills with the cross cascade gradient down to minus 6 to 8 mb by 12Z Wednesday. Increasing easterly winds in the foothills.

Cloud cover increasing quickly Wednesday morning as the next system begins to move inland well south of the area. Bands of showers rotating around the upper level low moving over Southern Washington could get as far north as Everett during the day. Breezy east winds continuing in the foothills. Highs near 50.

Upper level low weakening over Oregon Wednesday night into Thursday. High amplitude upper level ridge building offshore Thursday extending north into the Yukon. Dry northerly flow aloft developing over Western Washington decreasing cloud cover by Thursday afternoon. Lows in the mid 30s to lower 40s. Highs near 50.

sections.title: Long term (Thursday night through Monday)
paragraphs: Models in good agreement Thursday night into Friday with the high amplitude upper level ridge offshore moving over Western Washington Friday. Ridge gets pinched off Friday night as another system sets off off the coast. Models still having trouble coming to a consistent solution over the weekend. Some ensemble solutions take the system offshore and move it inland south of the area Saturday night into Sunday. Other ensemble solutions stall the system off the Washington coast. With a lack of a consensus will stay with the chance of rain forecast over the weekend. Snow levels around 2500 feet so any precipitation the Cascades get will be in the form of snow in the passes.

Inconsistencies in the solutions continue into Monday with a pair of possible solutions the leading contenders, one an upper level ridge building over the area and two what is left of the stalled system offshore moving through Western Washington. Ensemble solutions are no help keeping the broadbrush chance of rain forecast going into Monday. Snow levels remaining below pass levels.
Lows in the upper 20s and 30s Friday and Saturday morning, mid 30s to lower 40s Sunday and Monday morning. Highs near 50 through the period. Felton

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: A mix of VFR to MVFR conditions continue this morning across the terminals, with most fog clearing within the past couple of hours. Ceilings will improve to VFR through the morning, with ceilings scattering out this afternoon 17Z-20Z. Guidance hints at another round of lower-end VFR clouds with isolated fog in the Kitsap and mountains. Southeasterly winds this afternoon will transition southwesterly. Winds will transition northeasterly Tuesday evening, with easterly winds increasing Tuesday night into Wednesday morning, particularly through the Cascade gaps, Strait of Juan de Fuca, and HQM.

KSEA...VFR today. Expectation for Wednesday morning is for lower-end VFR clouds to roll in, with lower conditions (MVFR) favored west of the terminal. Southeasterly winds will transition southwesterly this afternoon around 5 kt. Winds will transition northeasterly this evening around 00Z, increasing to 6-9 kt.
29/HPR

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Winds expected to increase across the waters today and will turn offshore this evening as a low pressure system offshore moves southwards across the NE Pacific. Additionally, offshore winds will be locally enhanced along terrain gaps, particularly through the Strait of Juan de Fuca and near Grays Harbor Tuesday night. Small Craft Advisories have been issued for the West and Central Strait of Juan de Fuca, with latest high-res guidance indicating a 70-100% chance of small craft winds. Winds across the outer coastal waters expected to reach gale thresholds this afternoon, for which a Gale Warning has been issued. Gusts may also briefly reach gale along the inner coastal waters Wednesday morning at times, especially the waters adjacent to the West Entrance of the Strait of Juan de Fuca and Grays Harbor County. As of this morning, the Small Craft Advisory for the inner coastal waters has been extended through Wednesday morning. Seas will briefly decrease to 10 feet or below this afternoon, before increasing to to 10-15 feet Tuesday night into Wednesday.

As the low pressure system continues to push south into California and away from area waters, weak high pressure will build late Wednesday into Thursday for calmer marine conditions. An active weather pattern returns  this weekend into next week as multiple systems are expected to move over the waters.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: Dry conditions return today before another system approaches tonight into Wednesday, bringing light precipitation, mountain snow, and increasing easterly winds through the Gorge. Dry weather returns Thursday and Friday, with morning fog possible before a more unsettled pattern develops over the weekend.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Monday...A brief break in the active weather pattern is expected today as high pressure builds over the Pacific Northwest. Despite the return to dry conditions, lingering low-level moisture will support areas of morning fog across the interior valleys. The Willamette Valley and coastal valleys will be most susceptible, with locally reduced visibility possible during morning commute. Conditions should improve through the morning as daytime heating allows the fog to dissipate.

Attention then turns to a developing area of low pressure offshore tonight. As the low tracks south toward California, an associated frontal boundary will push toward the Oregon coast before weakening as it moves inland Wednesday. This southward trajectory should keep the more substantial precipitation south of the area, with the heaviest rainfall expected along the central Oregon coast and farther south. Northwest Oregon and southwest Washington should see comparatively lighter precipitation, with overall impacts from this system remaining limited.

The tightening pressure gradient ahead of the offshore low will also promote increasing easterly winds tonight into Wednesday morning. The Columbia River Gorge and eastern Portland metro are favored to see the strongest gusts, generally around 25-35 mph, with locally higher speeds possible near Corbett and other favored gap-wind locations.

Across the Cascades, snow levels are expected to fall to around 3000-4000 ft tonight into Wednesday, possibly as low as 2500 ft in areas such as the Upper Hood River Valley. This will bring some snow to the higher elevations, although accumulations at pass level currently appear modest. Probabilities for at least 3 inches of snow over a 24 hour period are around 15-20%. There is also a lower-end possibility, around 10%, that snow levels briefly drop toward 1000-1500 ft across the central Columbia River Gorge and Upper Hood River Valley. If this occurs, a few flurries could reach higher elevations near Parkdale, though significant accumulation at these elevations is not anticipated.

Conditions should settle down again Thursday as the system moves south and high pressure returns. Ensemble guidance supports an extended period of dry weather through Friday. The combination of light winds and lingering surface moisture will favor another round of morning valley fog, particularly Friday. The extent of fog development will depend in part on how much moisture remains following Wednesdays precipitation.

The forecast becomes less certain heading into the weekend as the next series of low pressure systems begin developing offshore. The signal for precipitation returning is still uncertain, with only 50% of the clusters showing precipitation by Saturday. Ensemble members suggest the lows will generally remain offshore of Oregon and Washington rather than tracking south toward California, which would favor periods of showers through Monday. While the pattern looks to become more active again, the potential for significant weather impacts across the region appears relatively low at this time. ~12

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 12Z Wednesday...Expect a mix of conditions throughout the airspace this morning, currently with low stratus/fog at a few terminals such as KHIO, KMMV, and KCVO, and VFR/MVFR conditions at all other terminals as of 11Z Tue. Expect conditions to gradually improve towards the afternoon, with a return of widespread VFR conditions by 19-20Z Tue. Confidence for MVFR or VFR conditions at other terminals is rather low, with just a 30-45% chance of MVFR CIGs at various terminals, therefore TAFs will largely rely on persistence of recent observations then probabilistic guidance. As for terminals under LIFR/IFR status, there is a moderate confidence for such conditions to continue as a result of recent observations and a 50-65% chance of LIFR/IFR conditions.

Looking ahead, high clouds increase from southwest to northeast around 06Z Wed as a frontal system approaches. This system will bring rain to the area, however rain is expected to hold off until after 06Z Wed.
Expect light and variable winds less than 5 kt through 18Z Tuesday. Offshore winds begin to increase towards 06Z Wed ahead of the aforementioned frontal system.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...Predominately VFR conditions with around a 30% chance for CIGs below 3500 ft through 17Z Tue. Winds remain light and variable through 00Z Wed, then increase to around 8-12 kt with gusts up to 22 kt after 06Z Wed. ~12

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Wave heights continue to gradually decrease this morning towards 10-12 ft for all marine zones. Conditions will still remain hazardous for small craft.

Winds and seas will ramp back up this afternoon and tonight as the next frontal system moves over the coastal waters, bringing southerly wind gusts up to 40 kt over the outer waters, with the highest gusts expected beyond 30 NM offshore. The inner waters will see relatively weaker winds from this incoming system, with gusts up to 30 kt. Therefore, Gale Warnings remain in effect for the outer waters this afternoon through tonight. Winds weaken Wednesday, but with seas remaining elevated around 12-16 ft at 14 seconds due to a fresh westerly swell. Calmer conditions arrive on Thursday with seas falling below 10 ft and relatively light offshore winds. Conditions look to ramp up once again this weekend as another system moves towards the coast, bringing southerly winds with gusts up to 30 kt and seas building towards 14-16 ft. ~12/23
